facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Debt at carrying value fell from USD 94,756 million at December 31, 2025 to USD 93,959 million at June 30, 2026, a fall of USD 797 million or 0.84%, while last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA fell from USD 22,611 million to USD 22,251 million, a fall of 1.59%. The debt reduction was smaller than the earnings decline, so Adjusted EBITDA leverage rose from 4.19 times to 4.22 times and net leverage from 4.18 times to 4.21 times. tables.title: Contrary evidence and what would change the view

rows.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view — paragraph 1
Chart data: revenue and EBITDA — paragraph 1

limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- Adjusted EBITDA for FY2023 is not stated in the supplied filings, which restricts the FY2023 point of the revenue and EBITDA table and any FY2023 margin or leverage; severity Low; the action that would close it is the FY2024 annual report, which would state it. - The filings print a dash for the noncontrolling interest share of income in the second quarter of 2025, the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, for deferred income taxes in the first half of 2025, for borrowings under the equipment installment plan financing facility in FY2023, for debt issuance costs in the first quarter of 2025, for loans payable to related parties in FY2024 and FY2025, for receivables from related party at June 30, 2026, for payables to related party at December 31, 2025 and for the current portion of long-term debt at March 31, 2026; each is shown as not supplied and none is read as zero; severity Low because every total is printed; the action is to confirm the nil meaning with the issuer. - A balance sheet at December 31, 2023 is not supplied, so FY2023 net debt, cash and leverage are not calculable; severity Low; the action is the FY2024 annual report, which would print the December 31, 2023 balance sheet. - Some lines are not printed in every filing: deferred income taxes in the first-quarter 2026 and 2025 cash flows, payables to related party and loans payable to related parties in most periods, and cash paid for income taxes outside the annual tax note and the nine-month 2025 and 2024 cash flow lines; the nine-month 2025 figure of USD 28 million exceeds the full-year 2025 net figure of USD 18 million and the filings do not explain the difference, which restricts any cash tax rate; severity Low; the action is to obtain a cash tax disclosure on one basis. - Discrete second-, third- and fourth-quarter cash flows are not printed, only period-to-date amounts, which restricts a quarterly cash flow trend; severity Low; the action is to derive quarters by subtraction and label them if a quarterly series is needed. - The fourth quarter of 2025 income statement is calculated as the year less nine months because the issuer prints no fourth-quarter statement and the parent's fourth quarter covers a different perimeter; severity Low; the action is to keep the label calculated. - Instrument-level debt terms, the maturity ladder, facility commitments, letters of credit (USD 364 million at year-end) and covenant levels are available only at December 31, 2025, while the June 30, 2026 report gives debt in three classes; this restricts the debt stack, the ladder and liquidity by facility at the latest date; severity Medium; the action is to obtain an instrument table at June 30, 2026 or the third-quarter 2026 report. - The credit facility tranche amounts are printed rounded (approximately USD 413 million, USD 4.3 billion, USD 729 million, USD 2.0 billion, USD 2.5 billion and USD 2.1 billion drawn on the revolving loan), they sum to USD 12,042 million against a printed credit facility principal of USD 11,949 million, a difference of USD 93 million, and tranche carrying values are not printed; the instrument register therefore exceeds Total Debt by USD 141 million, of which USD 48 million is unallocated facility financing cost; severity Low; the action is to obtain exact tranche balances. - The drawn amount of the Revolving Loan B of about USD 960 million maturing on August 31, 2027 is not stated; it matures within twelve months of the as-of date, which restricts the liquidity read; severity Medium; the action is to obtain the drawn balance from the credit agreement compliance data. - Availability under the credit facilities is printed to the nearest USD 0.1 billion and is not stated at December 31, 2024, so the FY2024 undrawn figure is not supplied and the other figures carry that rounding; severity Low; the action is to obtain exact availability. - The equipment installment plan financing facility is left out of the debt stack because its legal rank against the other debt is not stated and its assets are not available to other creditors; it, and USD 1,155 million of deferred payment program borrowings carried in accrued liabilities, are outside Total Debt, which restricts comparison with a measure that includes them; severity Medium; the action is to decide the debt definition for the analysis and use the sensitivity rows. - The issuer prints one reportable segment, so no segment revenue schedule exists beyond revenue by product line, and no segment sum is stated; severity Low; no action is needed. - The Cox Transactions and the Liberty Broadband Combination are pending at the latest filing and the Cox cash consideration is stated as USD 500 million in the annual report and USD 650 million in the 2026 quarterly reports; no pro forma adjustment is made and none of it is blended into period figures; severity Medium; the action is to obtain the amended transaction terms or a later filing. - Free cash flow and Adjusted EBITDA are the issuer's own non-GAAP definitions and the covenant definition of EBITDA excludes management fees paid to other Charter entities, so covenant capacity cannot be inferred; severity Medium; the action is to obtain the executed debt documents and the compliance calculation.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Creditors have no independent owner or management to rely on, because CCO Holdings is a holding company wholly owned by CCH I Holdings and Charter entities run its financing, cash management and treasury on a centralized basis. Protection therefore rests on the indenture tests: the indentures permit debt, dividends and investments in certain circumstances only while pro forma leverage stays below a specified level, the maximum total leverage ratio is 6.0 times, and the ratio was 4.0 times at December 31, 2025. A breach of the Charter Operating credit facility covenants, whose total leverage ratio stood at 2.8 times against a 5.0 times maximum at year-end, would also be an event of default on the issuer's debt. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence for a lower risk level is that parent behaviour has stayed within the indenture tests and no creditor-adverse action is documented: distributions were 91.96% of free cash flow across FY2023 to FY2025 and only 53.44% in FY2024, the indenture leverage ratio was 4.0 times against a 6.0 times maximum, the Charter Operating total leverage ratio was 2.8 times against a 5.0 times maximum, maturities were extended without an exchange offer, the issuer's debt was repurchased below par, and Charter's long-term leverage target has fallen to 3.5 times. facts.text: Charter, Charter Holdings and Cox Enterprises signed the Transaction Agreement on May 16, 2025. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Liquidity and near-term maturities are comfortable, and refinancing is a cost issue rather than an access issue: cash and undrawn facilities of USD 3,985 million cover the maturities of 2026 and 2027 that remain after the February 2026 redemption about 2.48 times, and the January 2026 issue of USD 3,000 million showed open market access, although availability fell from USD 4.6 billion to USD 3.7 billion in the second quarter as credit facility principal rose USD 788 million while note principal fell USD 1,245 million, a pattern consistent with revolver-funded note repurchases that the filings do not explain. The USD 11,300 million of unsecured notes due 2028 to 2030 carry a weighted coupon of 5.04% against 7.16% on the January 2026 notes, so refinancing them at those coupons would add USD 238.78 million of annual interest and lower cover to 4.23 times from 4.43 times. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest case for a better view is that leverage has held in a narrow range, cash interest is covered 4.43 times, mobile growth is replacing declining lines, distributions were 91.96% of free cash flow across FY2023 to FY2025, and the capital programme that depresses free cash flow ends around 2027, so conversion could improve without any earnings growth. The view would move toward strong if capital expenditure fell after 2027 and the parent let free cash flow reduce debt, and toward weak if Adjusted EBITDA kept falling at the first-half rate while distributions stayed near free cash flow, which would take leverage to 4.36 times at constant debt and to 4.51 times at twice that rate. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; calculation F2; calculation F15; calculation F16

facts.label: Company description
facts.text: CCO Holdings is a holding company whose operating subsidiaries sell subscription Internet, mobile, video and voice services under the Spectrum brand to residential and business customers across 41 states, and its revenue is overwhelmingly recurring, with residential services at 76.85% of first-half 2026 revenue. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is recurring and subscription based but no longer growing: reported revenue fell 0.56% in FY2025 and 1.37% in the first half of 2026, and excluding the seamless entertainment allocation the first-half decline was -0.08%. Beneath that, Internet revenue fell 2.28%, video revenue fell 9.44% and voice revenue fell 4.70% while mobile service revenue grew 17.00% and advertising revenue grew 8.86% in an election year, so mobile and advertising are offsetting broadband and video. Pricing power is limited: reported revenue per residential customer fell 1.82% while the company pursues lower promotional and persistent bundled prices, and fiber to the home competitors overlap about 27% and 16% of the footprint. Revenue is therefore predictable near term but structurally declining in video and broadband customers, which caps earnings growth. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Programming is the largest cost line at 26.87% of FY2025 operating costs and expenses, followed by other costs of revenue at 20.42%, so nearly half of costs move with video and mobile volumes: programming fees are generally paid per customer and fall as video customers leave, while other costs rise with mobile growth. In the first half of 2026 programming fell USD 432 million, of which USD 355 million was the seamless entertainment allocation that also lowered revenue, while other costs of revenue rose USD 367 million and transition costs added USD 89 million; cost growth excluding the allocation was USD 337 million against flat underlying revenue. Margins can be defended against volume loss through programming savings, but not against mobile cost growth and integration spend, which is why Adjusted EBITDA fell 3.16% on flat underlying revenue. facts.text: Capital expenditure was 22.18% of revenue for the twelve months to June 30, 2026 against 21.22% in FY2025, which includes the network evolution programme and subsidized rural construction of USD 818 million in the first half of 2026, and the parent, Charter, expects about USD 11.4 billion of capital expenditure in 2026 excluding Cox. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The downside path starts with continued Internet customer and video losses and mobile and integration cost growth, so that Adjusted EBITDA keeps falling at the first-half rate of 3.16%. At that rate last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA would be USD 21,548 million, leverage 4.36 times at constant debt, cash interest cover 4.29 times and free cash flow USD 4,367 million, and at twice that rate USD 20,845 million, 4.51 times, 4.15 times and USD 3,664 million. Free cash flow after distributions is already negative over the last twelve months, so a further fall would force the parent to cut distributions or add debt, the first break would be financial policy rather than a liquidity shortfall, and management levers are lower distributions, slower rural construction, capital spending after 2027 and revolver availability. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress over 12 to 24 months because liquidity covers the remaining 2026 and 2027 maturities 2.48 times, but leverage would drift toward 4.5 times, which leaves the unsecured notes, ranking behind the secured debt, most exposed. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, CCO Holdings presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, recurring revenue and a 41.28% Adjusted EBITDA margin, but credit quality is constrained by leverage of 4.22 times that is not falling, a parent that takes all or nearly all free cash flow and unsecured notes that sit behind guaranteed and secured debt. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because interest is covered 4.43 times, although conversion fell to 22.79% of Adjusted EBITDA. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on market access for the 2028 to 2030 maturities, which are 28.05% of principal and would cost more at today's coupons, and on whether the Cox cash payment adds secured debt. The primary downside path is falling broadband customers and rising costs compressing earnings while distributions continue. Further analysis would require the executed debt documents, Cox earnings and savings, and a peer set for relative assessment. Fundamental credit analysis is complete with limitations, and the top risk is the parent's cash sweep alongside shrinking earnings. Balances, earnings and liquidity at June 30, 2026 can be read from the issuer's own statements. ## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage is stable but not improving: debt of USD 93,959 million was 4.22 times last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA at June 30, 2026, against 4.19 times at December 31, 2025, because a USD 797 million reduction in debt only partly offset falling earnings.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 26; calculation C48; calculation C49

On reported EBITDA, which the issuer does not state and which is derived here from operating income, the figures are 4.41 times at both dates. Interest on a cash-paid basis was covered 4.43 times by last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA. Almost all of the half-year's free cash flow went to the parent company as distributions, so internal cash flow is not reducing debt. Liquidity rests on about USD 3,700 million of undrawn facilities and USD 285 million of cash.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 26; calculation C60; calculation C58
### Key findings

Debt at carrying value fell from USD 94,756 million at December 31, 2025 to USD 93,959 million at June 30, 2026, a fall of USD 797 million or 0.84%, while last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA fell from USD 22,611 million to USD 22,251 million, a fall of 1.59%. The debt reduction was smaller than the earnings decline, so Adjusted EBITDA leverage rose from 4.19 times to 4.22 times and net leverage from 4.18 times to 4.21 times. Second-quarter Adjusted EBITDA was 4.23% lower than a year earlier, so holding leverage near 4.2 times depends on continued debt reduction rather than on earnings recovery.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 26; calculation C48; calculation C63; calculation C50; calculation C51; calculation C59

Free cash flow on the issuer's definition was USD 2,492 million in the first half of 2026 against USD 3,249 million a year earlier, a fall of 23.30%, because Adjusted EBITDA fell by USD 360 million and capital expenditure rose by USD 440 million. Distributions to the parent were USD 2,460 million in the same half-year, 98.72% of free cash flow, so the cash the business generates is passed up to the parent. The USD 498 million by which repayments of long-term debt exceeded borrowings therefore had to come from other sources, and the quarterly report attributes the lower financing outflow partly to higher short-term borrowings under the deferred payment program. Creditors depend on lower distributions or higher earnings, not on retained cash, for deleveraging.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 36; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 37; calculation C52; calculation C53; calculation C58; calculation C65

Adjusted EBITDA exceeds EBITDA derived from reported operating income by the add-backs of stock compensation of USD 673 million and other operating expenses of USD 432 million in FY2025, which together are USD 1,105 million, so leverage on reported EBITDA is 4.41 times rather than 4.19 times. The covenant measure adds back a further management fee of USD 1.4 billion that is paid to other Charter entities, which is consistent with the indenture leverage of 4.0 times reported at year-end, below both figures shown here.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 91; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 156; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 167; calculation C47; calculation C42

About USD 3,700 million was undrawn under the credit facilities at June 30, 2026, USD 900 million less than the USD 4,600 million at March 31, 2026, and cash was USD 285 million. The filings do not state why availability fell, and facility commitments and letters of credit are known only at year-end, so liquidity cannot be rebuilt facility by facility at the latest date.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-03-31_ccoh-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation C64

The equipment installment plan financing facility of USD 1,596 million and USD 1,155 million of deferred payment program borrowings are carried outside the issuer's debt total and together add USD 2,751 million, which would lift Adjusted EBITDA leverage to 4.35 times. Supplier finance of USD 725 million is a further funding source that sits in payables.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 10; calculation C54; calculation C55

At year-end USD 31,149 million, or 32.92% of principal, was due by 2030, with 2030 the largest single year. The January 2026 issue of USD 3,000 million of notes and the February 2026 redemption of USD 3,000 million of notes moved near-term maturities out to 2033 and 2036, so the year-end ladder overstates the maturities of 2026 and 2027.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 104; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 160; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation C39; calculation C56
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest counter-argument is that leverage has held between 4.18 times and 4.22 times on Adjusted EBITDA across five balance-sheet dates and that the indenture test was met with room, at 4.0 times against a 6.0 times maximum at year-end. Free cash flow was USD 5,827 million in FY2025. The view would improve if distributions to the parent fell below free cash flow, and weaken if last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA fell to USD 22,000 million without a matching fall in debt, which would take leverage to 4.27 times.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 91–92; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 156; calculation C57
### Limitations
- Instrument terms, facility commitments, letters of credit and covenant levels are available only at December 31, 2025; the June 30, 2026 quarterly report gives debt in three classes.
- EBITDA on a reported basis is derived from operating income and depreciation and amortization, and Adjusted EBITDA is the issuer's own definition, not stated for FY2023.
- Interim figures are unaudited, and the fourth quarter of 2025 is calculated as the year less nine months.

## Gaps

- Adjusted EBITDA for FY2023 is not stated in the supplied filings, which restricts the FY2023 point of the revenue and EBITDA table and any FY2023 margin or leverage; severity Low; the action that would close it is the FY2024 annual report, which would state it.

- The filings print a dash for the noncontrolling interest share of income in the second quarter of 2025, the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, for deferred income taxes in the first half of 2025, for borrowings under the equipment installment plan financing facility in FY2023, for debt issuance costs in the first quarter of 2025, for loans payable to related parties in FY2024 and FY2025, for receivables from related party at June 30, 2026, for payables to related party at December 31, 2025 and for the current portion of long-term debt at March 31, 2026; each is shown as not supplied and none is read as zero; severity Low because every total is printed; the action is to confirm the nil meaning with the issuer.

- A balance sheet at December 31, 2023 is not supplied, so FY2023 net debt, cash and leverage are not calculable; severity Low; the action is the FY2024 annual report, which would print the December 31, 2023 balance sheet.

- Some lines are not printed in every filing: deferred income taxes in the first-quarter 2026 and 2025 cash flows, payables to related party and loans payable to related parties in most periods, and cash paid for income taxes outside the annual tax note and the nine-month 2025 and 2024 cash flow lines; the nine-month 2025 figure of USD 28 million exceeds the full-year 2025 net figure of USD 18 million and the filings do not explain the difference, which restricts any cash tax rate; severity Low; the action is to obtain a cash tax disclosure on one basis.

- Discrete second-, third- and fourth-quarter cash flows are not printed, only period-to-date amounts, which restricts a quarterly cash flow trend; severity Low; the action is to derive quarters by subtraction and label them if a quarterly series is needed.

- The fourth quarter of 2025 income statement is calculated as the year less nine months because the issuer prints no fourth-quarter statement and the parent's fourth quarter covers a different perimeter; severity Low; the action is to keep the label calculated.

- Instrument-level debt terms, the maturity ladder, facility commitments, letters of credit (USD 364 million at year-end) and covenant levels are available only at December 31, 2025, while the June 30, 2026 report gives debt in three classes; this restricts the debt stack, the ladder and liquidity by facility at the latest date; severity Medium; the action is to obtain an instrument table at June 30, 2026 or the third-quarter 2026 report.

- The credit facility tranche amounts are printed rounded (approximately USD 413 million, USD 4.3 billion, USD 729 million, USD 2.0 billion, USD 2.5 billion and USD 2.1 billion drawn on the revolving loan), they sum to USD 12,042 million against a printed credit facility principal of USD 11,949 million, a difference of USD 93 million, and tranche carrying values are not printed; the instrument register therefore exceeds Total Debt by USD 141 million, of which USD 48 million is unallocated facility financing cost; severity Low; the action is to obtain exact tranche balances.

- The drawn amount of the Revolving Loan B of about USD 960 million maturing on August 31, 2027 is not stated; it matures within twelve months of the as-of date, which restricts the liquidity read; severity Medium; the action is to obtain the drawn balance from the credit agreement compliance data.

- Availability under the credit facilities is printed to the nearest USD 0.1 billion and is not stated at December 31, 2024, so the FY2024 undrawn figure is not supplied and the other figures carry that rounding; severity Low; the action is to obtain exact availability.

- The equipment installment plan financing facility is left out of the debt stack because its legal rank against the other debt is not stated and its assets are not available to other creditors; it, and USD 1,155 million of deferred payment program borrowings carried in accrued liabilities, are outside Total Debt, which restricts comparison with a measure that includes them; severity Medium; the action is to decide the debt definition for the analysis and use the sensitivity rows.
- The issuer prints one reportable segment, so no segment revenue schedule exists beyond revenue by product line, and no segment sum is stated; severity Low; no action is needed.

- The Cox Transactions and the Liberty Broadband Combination are pending at the latest filing and the Cox cash consideration is stated as USD 500 million in the annual report and USD 650 million in the 2026 quarterly reports; no pro forma adjustment is made and none of it is blended into period figures; severity Medium; the action is to obtain the amended transaction terms or a later filing.

- Free cash flow and Adjusted EBITDA are the issuer's own non-GAAP definitions and the covenant definition of EBITDA excludes management fees paid to other Charter entities, so covenant capacity cannot be inferred; severity Medium; the action is to obtain the executed debt documents and the compliance calculation.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Sponsor and governance risk for CCO Holdings creditors is Medium: the issuer is a wholly owned, centrally managed Charter subsidiary whose cash is passed to the parent, and two unclosed transactions would add debt and change Charter's owners. Distributions to the parent were USD 2,460 million in the first half of 2026 against free cash flow of USD 2,492 million, and USD 6,794 million in FY2025 against USD 5,827 million.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 142; calculation C8; calculation C9

The Cox Transactions require about USD 4.2 billion of cash at closing, which the issuer's reports say will be funded with debt that may rank as guaranteed and secured, and neither they nor the Liberty Broadband Combination had closed at the latest filing. The filings state the cash consideration differently, so the size of the new debt is not established.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 34; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 52; EX-99.1_2026-07-24_chtrex991earningsrelease63.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation C13
### Key findings

Creditors have no independent owner or management to rely on, because CCO Holdings is a holding company wholly owned by CCH I Holdings and Charter entities run its financing, cash management and treasury on a centralized basis. Protection therefore rests on the indenture tests: the indentures permit debt, dividends and investments in certain circumstances only while pro forma leverage stays below a specified level, the maximum total leverage ratio is 6.0 times, and the ratio was 4.0 times at December 31, 2025. A breach of the Charter Operating credit facility covenants, whose total leverage ratio stood at 2.8 times against a 5.0 times maximum at year-end, would also be an event of default on the issuer's debt.

Cash generated by the business is passed to the parent: distributions were 98.72% of first-half 2026 free cash flow and 116.60% in FY2025, when they exceeded free cash flow by USD 967 million while principal debt rose by USD 838 million. The filings state that CCO Holdings and its subsidiaries are the primary source of funding for Charter's market share repurchases through distributions to their parent companies, so deleveraging of the issuer depends on the parent choosing to distribute less.

Standing repurchase arrangements add parent-level cash demands whose funding entity the filings do not state: each month Charter must buy Liberty Broadband shares worth the greater of USD 100 million and a minimum liquidity amount, or lend that amount where a purchase is not possible, and it bought USD 595 million of shares in the first half of 2026 and advanced a term loan of about USD 359 million in May 2026. A/N has suspended its own sales to Charter until the Cox Transactions close or end, which removes a second claim for now but can be reversed by A/N.

The Cox Transactions are the largest change to leverage and ranking risk: Charter must fund about USD 4.2 billion of cash at closing with new debt, which the issuer's own report says may be guaranteed and secured, and will assume about USD 12.4 billion of Cox net debt and finance leases whose unsecured notes are expected to become guaranteed and secured debt. The issuer's unsecured notes, 28.49% of principal debt at June 30, 2026, are not covered by those guarantees and are structurally subordinated, so a larger pool of guaranteed and secured debt would sit ahead of them. The annual report describes a split credit rating in which the secured notes are investment grade and the unsecured notes, USD 27.3 billion at year-end, are high yield.

These are rights at Charter, not at CCO Holdings, and the filings describe no creditor-specific consent right attached to them; whether either transaction triggers the 101% change of control offer in the issuer's notes is not stated.

Financial policy is set at Charter's level and points to lower leverage after closing: Charter's net leverage was 4.18 times at June 30, 2026, it plans to stay near the midpoint of its range of 4.0 times to 4.5 times until closing, and its stated long-term target has narrowed from a range of 3.5 times to 4.0 times in the third-quarter 2025 report to 3.5 times in the second-quarter 2026 report, with a stated expectation of reducing total debt to get there. ### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence for a lower risk level is that parent behaviour has stayed within the indenture tests and no creditor-adverse action is documented: distributions were 91.96% of free cash flow across FY2023 to FY2025 and only 53.44% in FY2024, the indenture leverage ratio was 4.0 times against a 6.0 times maximum, the Charter Operating total leverage ratio was 2.8 times against a 5.0 times maximum, maturities were extended without an exchange offer, the issuer's debt was repurchased below par, and Charter's long-term leverage target has fallen to 3.5 times. The view would move toward Low if the Cox Transactions close with the new debt sized to Charter's stated target while distributions fall below free cash flow, and toward High if distributions continue at or above free cash flow after closing while guaranteed and secured debt grows ahead of the issuer's unsecured notes.

### Limitations

- The entity that funds the Liberty Broadband repurchases, the May 2026 loan and the Cox cash payment is not stated, so the finding that these claims fall on cash distributed by the issuer rests on Charter's general statement about repurchase funding and could be overstated.

- Ownership percentages inside the Charter group appear only in a chart that the supplied text does not carry, so the ownership map shows those links without percentages and the extent of Charter's economic interest in the issuer's parent chain is not established.

- Shareholder, antitrust and regulatory approval status and the closing date of the Cox Transactions are not stated in any supplied filing, so the Medium rating assumes both transactions remain open and would change on closing.

- Executed indentures and credit agreements are not supplied, so capacity to pay distributions, add secured debt or release guarantees is judged only from the leverage test the filings state, and capacity cannot be separated from willingness beyond that.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

Charter, Charter Holdings and Cox Enterprises signed the Transaction Agreement on May 16, 2025. At closing Charter pays USD 3.5 billion in cash for Cox's commercial fiber and managed IT and cloud businesses, and Charter Holdings pays Cox Enterprises USD 650 million in cash, issues USD 6.0 billion of convertible preferred units and common units, and receives Cox's residential cable business; Charter also issues one share of a new Class C common stock to Cox Enterprises whose votes reflect its as-converted holdings of Charter Holdings units. The preferred units carry a fixed annual dividend worth USD 412.5 million, and the combined entity assumes about USD 12.4 billion of Cox net debt and finance leases. The annual report instead states the Charter Holdings cash as USD 500 million and the assumed net debt as USD 12.6 billion, so the terms are recorded with all figures in the conflict log.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation C13; calculation C14

The Liberty Broadband Combination, agreed on November 12, 2024, would make Liberty Broadband an indirect wholly owned Charter subsidiary and is expected to close with the Cox Transactions. Liberty Broadband's preferred stock would convert into Charter preferred stock with a mandatory redemption date in 2039, and Charter bears the corporate-level tax on the divestiture of GCI, completed on July 14, 2025, with tax benefits realized by GCI shared back to Charter for any liability above USD 420 million.

New debt has been raised and replaced at the Charter Operating and issuer levels. In September 2025 Charter Operating issued USD 1,250 million of 2035 senior secured notes and USD 750 million of 2055 senior secured notes. In January 2026 the issuer and its co-issuer sold USD 1,750 million of 2033 senior notes and USD 1,250 million of 2036 senior notes, and in February 2026 redeemed USD 750 million of 2026 notes and USD 2,250 million of 2027 notes. The Cox cash payment is the next financing: about USD 4.2 billion of new debt is described as guaranteed and secured only when issued, so its issue date, issuer and terms are not established. The equipment installment plan financing facility was amended in November 2025 to allow borrowing of up to USD 2.0 billion and carried USD 1.6 billion at June 30, 2026.

# Fundamental credit for CCO HOLDINGS LLC
## Request

CCO HOLDINGS LLC (issuer id cco-holdings-llc), as of 2026-11-05, credit snapshot pathway. This assessment synthesizes the issuer's fundamental credit profile from the financial foundation and the business and governance analysis, with checks against the filings, and does not assign a rating or a security view.
## Sources

## Findings
### Bottom line

Fundamental credit quality is adequate but not improving: Adjusted EBITDA covers cash interest 4.43 times, yet leverage of 4.22 times is not falling because earnings are drifting lower and the parent takes all or nearly all free cash flow. Creditors therefore depend on lower parent distributions, not earnings growth, to reduce leverage. The primary downside path is continued broadband customer losses and cost growth, which at the first-half rate of earnings decline would lift leverage to 4.36 times.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F2; calculation F15

Liquidity of USD 3,985 million covers the 2026 and 2027 maturities that remain 2.48 times, so near-term distress is unlikely; the larger risk is the 2028 to 2030 maturities, which are 28.05% of principal and, for the unsecured notes, would cost USD 238.78 million more a year at the January 2026 coupons.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-03-31_ccoh-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 27; calculation F12; calculation F13; calculation F14
### Key findings

Scale and recurring subscription revenue are the strongest credit support: FY2025 revenue of USD 54,774 million earned an Adjusted EBITDA margin of 41.28%, last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA covers cash interest paid 4.43 times, and only about 13% of borrowings carried variable rates at year-end, so interest cost reacts slowly to market moves. Cash generation of this kind keeps debt service secure while earnings stay near current levels.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 87–88; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 52; calculation F1; calculation F2

Revenue durability is the weakest operating dimension, but the reported revenue decline overstates it: Internet customers fell 1.74% over twelve months and reported revenue per residential customer fell 1.82%, yet excluding the seamless entertainment allocation, which lowers video revenue and programming cost by the same amount, first-half 2026 revenue was about flat at -0.08% against the reported 1.37% fall. Mobile service revenue grew 17.00% and video revenue fell 9.44%, and fiber to the home competitors overlap about 27% and 16% of the footprint, so growth in mobile is replacing declining broadband and video revenue rather than lifting the total. The Business & governance analysis reports the revenue decline without this adjustment.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 21; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 24; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 22; calculation F9; calculation F17; calculation F19

Earnings are falling because costs are rising against flat underlying revenue: in the first half of 2026 other costs of revenue rose USD 367 million with mobile device sales and direct service costs and transition costs for the Cox integration added USD 89 million, so Adjusted EBITDA fell 3.16% and the margin slipped to 40.73% from 41.47%. Transition costs are tied to the Cox integration and continue until it is complete, and mobile growth keeps adding device cost, so margin recovery is not assured and leverage cannot be reduced through earnings growth.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 14; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 24; calculation F9; calculation F11

Free cash flow is conversion-limited by heavy capital spending: last-twelve-months free cash flow of USD 5,070 million was 12.99% below FY2025 and 22.79% of Adjusted EBITDA against 25.77%, with capital expenditure at 22.18% of revenue, so Adjusted EBITDA less capital expenditure covers cash interest only 2.03 times. The network upgrade is largely complete by the end of 2027, which is the earliest point at which capital intensity could ease.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; calculation F3; calculation F4; calculation F5; calculation F6; calculation F7

Leverage is stable but not falling because the parent takes the cash: total debt was 4.22 times Adjusted EBITDA at June 30, 2026 against 4.19 times at December 31, 2025, and distributions to the parent were 98.72% of first-half 2026 free cash flow after exceeding it in FY2025, and were 116.33% over the last twelve months, leaving USD -828 million after distributions. Deleveraging therefore depends on the parent's choices, and Charter's stated long-term leverage target of 3.5 times after the Cox closing is supportive but is a parent-level target.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 27; calculation F2; calculation F16; calculation F18

Liquidity and near-term maturities are comfortable, and refinancing is a cost issue rather than an access issue: cash and undrawn facilities of USD 3,985 million cover the maturities of 2026 and 2027 that remain after the February 2026 redemption about 2.48 times, and the January 2026 issue of USD 3,000 million showed open market access, although availability fell from USD 4.6 billion to USD 3.7 billion in the second quarter as credit facility principal rose USD 788 million while note principal fell USD 1,245 million, a pattern consistent with revolver-funded note repurchases that the filings do not explain. The USD 11,300 million of unsecured notes due 2028 to 2030 carry a weighted coupon of 5.04% against 7.16% on the January 2026 notes, so refinancing them at those coupons would add USD 238.78 million of annual interest and lower cover to 4.23 times from 4.43 times.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 104; 10-Q_2026-03-31_ccoh-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-Q_2026-03-31_ccoh-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 10; calculation F13; calculation F14; calculation F20

Structure and governance add risk beyond the operating picture: the issuer's unsecured notes, 28.49% of principal debt, are not guaranteed and are structurally subordinated, a debt-funded Cox cash payment of about USD 4.2 billion may rank ahead of them, and Business & governance rates sponsor and governance risk Medium. The annual report describes a split rating in which the secured notes are investment grade and the unsecured notes are high yield, so the unsecured layer carries the structural and policy risk.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 92; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation F17
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case for a better view is that leverage has held in a narrow range, cash interest is covered 4.43 times, mobile growth is replacing declining lines, distributions were 91.96% of free cash flow across FY2023 to FY2025, and the capital programme that depresses free cash flow ends around 2027, so conversion could improve without any earnings growth. The view would move toward strong if capital expenditure fell after 2027 and the parent let free cash flow reduce debt, and toward weak if Adjusted EBITDA kept falling at the first-half rate while distributions stayed near free cash flow, which would take leverage to 4.36 times at constant debt and to 4.51 times at twice that rate.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; calculation F2; calculation F15; calculation F16
### Limitations

- The downside and refinancing figures hold debt, capital expenditure and cash interest constant and take rates from the issuer's own January 2026 issue, so they show direction and scale rather than a forecast, and a change in capital spending after the network upgrade would move the conclusions on the primary downside path.

- The seamless entertainment allocation is reported only as a change in costs netted within video revenue, so the revenue and cost split excluding it is calculated here and the finding that earnings pressure is a cost and mix problem rests on that calculation.

- Customer churn and retention are not stated and competitor overlap is given for only two footprint shares, so the view that revenue durability is the weakest dimension rests on net customer trends and could be too mild or too severe.

- Earnings, customers and savings of Cox Communications are not in the supplied filings, so the credit effect of closing cannot be sized and the adequate assessment applies to the issuer on a stand-alone basis.
- No peer set or market pricing is supplied, so the profile cannot be compared with other leveraged cable issuers and the adequate assessment is absolute rather than relative.
### Company description

CCO Holdings is a holding company whose operating subsidiaries sell subscription Internet, mobile, video and voice services under the Spectrum brand to residential and business customers across 41 states, and its revenue is overwhelmingly recurring, with residential services at 76.85% of first-half 2026 revenue. Recurring revenue gives visible cash flow for debt service, but the business needs heavy network investment and faces intense competition, and a single reportable segment means no part of it can be isolated for credit purposes.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 166; calculation F17
### Ownership and group structure

The issuer is wholly owned through CCH I Holdings by Charter, so financial policy is set at the parent: distributions were 98.72% of first-half 2026 free cash flow and 116.60% in FY2025, and Business & governance rates sponsor and governance risk Medium because two pending transactions would add debt and change Charter's owners. The unsecured notes, 28.49% of principal debt, are structurally subordinated to the guaranteed and secured debt, which may grow if the Cox cash payment is debt financed as the filings describe.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation F16; calculation F17
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is recurring and subscription based but no longer growing: reported revenue fell 0.56% in FY2025 and 1.37% in the first half of 2026, and excluding the seamless entertainment allocation the first-half decline was -0.08%. Beneath that, Internet revenue fell 2.28%, video revenue fell 9.44% and voice revenue fell 4.70% while mobile service revenue grew 17.00% and advertising revenue grew 8.86% in an election year, so mobile and advertising are offsetting broadband and video. Pricing power is limited: reported revenue per residential customer fell 1.82% while the company pursues lower promotional and persistent bundled prices, and fiber to the home competitors overlap about 27% and 16% of the footprint. Revenue is therefore predictable near term but structurally declining in video and broadband customers, which caps earnings growth.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Programming is the largest cost line at 26.87% of FY2025 operating costs and expenses, followed by other costs of revenue at 20.42%, so nearly half of costs move with video and mobile volumes: programming fees are generally paid per customer and fall as video customers leave, while other costs rise with mobile growth. In the first half of 2026 programming fell USD 432 million, of which USD 355 million was the seamless entertainment allocation that also lowered revenue, while other costs of revenue rose USD 367 million and transition costs added USD 89 million; cost growth excluding the allocation was USD 337 million against flat underlying revenue. Margins can be defended against volume loss through programming savings, but not against mobile cost growth and integration spend, which is why Adjusted EBITDA fell 3.16% on flat underlying revenue.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 166; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 14; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 24; calculation F9; calculation F10; calculation F11
### Capital intensity and FCF conversion

Capital expenditure was 22.18% of revenue for the twelve months to June 30, 2026 against 21.22% in FY2025, which includes the network evolution programme and subsidized rural construction of USD 818 million in the first half of 2026, and the parent, Charter, expects about USD 11.4 billion of capital expenditure in 2026 excluding Cox. Free cash flow converted 22.79% of Adjusted EBITDA against 25.77% in FY2025, cash interest took 22.58% of Adjusted EBITDA, and after capital expenditure Adjusted EBITDA covered cash interest 2.03 times. EBITDA therefore turns into free cash flow of about USD 5,070 million a year, which is enough to service debt but, with distributions near free cash flow, not enough to reduce it.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 19; EX-99.1_2026-07-24_chtrex991earningsrelease63.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; calculation F3; calculation F5; calculation F6; calculation F7; calculation F8; calculation F16
### Porter's five forces

Rivalry is intense and is the main force on revenue: fiber to the home competitors AT&T and Verizon overlap about 27% and 16% of the footprint, and Internet customers fell 1.74% over twelve months, so rivalry caps revenue and margin growth and leaves leverage reduction to cash retention.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 22; calculation F17

New entrants and substitutes arrive through fixed wireless access from mobile network operators, satellite, DSL and publicly subsidized or open access networks, and video faces streaming substitutes, which is why video revenue fell 9.44%; the threat raises the risk that Internet losses accelerate beyond the current rate.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 22; calculation F17; calculation F19

Buyer power is individually low but visible in pricing: the company uses lower promotional and persistent bundled pricing to drive growth, and reported revenue per residential customer fell 1.82%, which limits pricing as a lever for earnings.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 18; calculation F17

Supplier power is concentrated in programmers and in the mobile network: consolidation has left fewer programming suppliers with more selling power, programming was 25% of operating costs in the first half of 2026, and mobile service runs as a virtual operator on Verizon's network, so supplier cost increases pass into margin.
### PEST analysis
PEST factors do not appear to be a primary credit driver based on the provided materials beyond the competitive, regulatory and technology points covered under the five forces.
### SWOT analysis

Strengths are scale and recurring subscription revenue with a 41.28% Adjusted EBITDA margin in FY2025, cash interest covered 4.43 times, mostly fixed-rate borrowings and access to the debt market shown by the January 2026 issue.

### Strengths and weaknesses

The first strength is cash generation: Adjusted EBITDA of USD 22,251 million at a 40.91% margin for the twelve months covers cash interest of USD 5,024 million 4.43 times, so recurring subscription revenue translates into reliable debt service and supports an adequate profile.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F1; calculation F2

The second strength is debt structure and market access: only about 13% of borrowings are variable, the January 2026 issue of USD 3,000 million extended maturities, and the annual report describes a split rating, so refinancing is available at a higher cost rather than blocked.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 52; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 104; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 92; calculation F14
The third strength is liquidity: cash and undrawn facilities of USD 3,985 million cover the 2026 and 2027 maturities that remain 2.48 times, so no maturity pressure arises before 2028.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-Q_2026-03-31_ccoh-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation F13

The first weakness is the cash sweep: distributions took 98.72% of first-half 2026 free cash flow, 116.60% in FY2025 and 116.33% over the last twelve months, so leverage held at 4.22 times cannot fall without a change in parent policy.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F2; calculation F16

The second weakness is earnings direction: Adjusted EBITDA fell 3.16% in the first half on flat underlying revenue because costs rose, so the profile weakens if mobile and integration costs do not stabilize.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation F9
The third weakness is free cash flow conversion: capital expenditure at 22.18% of revenue cut conversion to 22.79% of Adjusted EBITDA, so earnings changes pass quickly into free cash flow.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F3; calculation F5; calculation F6

The fourth weakness is ranking and structure: the unsecured notes are 28.49% of principal debt, are not guaranteed and may sit behind new guaranteed and secured debt if the Cox cash payment is debt financed.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation F17
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months earnings are more likely to be flat to lower than higher: headwinds are continued broadband and video customer losses, contractual programming rate increases, mobile device and service costs and transition costs for the Cox integration, while tailwinds are mobile service growth of 17.00%, advertising revenue that rises in election years and the fall in programming cost as video customers decline. This outlook supports unchanged leverage at best, so the rate at which debt falls will depend on parent distributions.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 24; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 21; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 23; calculation F9; calculation F19

Over three to five years the network evolution should be complete by the end of 2027, which could lower capital intensity and lift free cash flow, while the refinancing of the 2028 to 2030 maturities at current rates would add about USD 238.78 million a year on the unsecured notes and the Cox Transactions, if completed, would add debt and scale that the supplied filings do not size. Company-specific tailwinds and headwinds therefore broadly offset, which keeps the view at adequate rather than improving.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccoh-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F12; calculation F14
### Downside scenario

The downside path starts with continued Internet customer and video losses and mobile and integration cost growth, so that Adjusted EBITDA keeps falling at the first-half rate of 3.16%. At that rate last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA would be USD 21,548 million, leverage 4.36 times at constant debt, cash interest cover 4.29 times and free cash flow USD 4,367 million, and at twice that rate USD 20,845 million, 4.51 times, 4.15 times and USD 3,664 million. Free cash flow after distributions is already negative over the last twelve months, so a further fall would force the parent to cut distributions or add debt, the first break would be financial policy rather than a liquidity shortfall, and management levers are lower distributions, slower rural construction, capital spending after 2027 and revolver availability. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress over 12 to 24 months because liquidity covers the remaining 2026 and 2027 maturities 2.48 times, but leverage would drift toward 4.5 times, which leaves the unsecured notes, ranking behind the secured debt, most exposed.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccoh-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-Q_2026-03-31_ccoh-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation F4; calculation F13; calculation F15; calculation F16
### Overall credit view

Overall, CCO Holdings presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, recurring revenue and a 41.28% Adjusted EBITDA margin, but credit quality is constrained by leverage of 4.22 times that is not falling, a parent that takes all or nearly all free cash flow and unsecured notes that sit behind guaranteed and secured debt. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because interest is covered 4.43 times, although conversion fell to 22.79% of Adjusted EBITDA. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on market access for the 2028 to 2030 maturities, which are 28.05% of principal and would cost more at today's coupons, and on whether the Cox cash payment adds secured debt. The primary downside path is falling broadband customers and rising costs compressing earnings while distributions continue. Further analysis would require the executed debt documents, Cox earnings and savings, and a peer set for relative assessment. Fundamental credit analysis is complete with limitations, and the top risk is the parent's cash sweep alongside shrinking earnings.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F2; calculation F3; calculation F12; calculation F15; calculation F16
